Research indicates that most current approaches struggle with accurately interpreting ambiguous cues like video captions or category names. To improve performance and reliability, our work focuses on building context through dynamic modeling of video sequences and object relationships. By incorporating self-supervised training and self-calibration, our system enhances the accuracy of action detection. Results show significant improvement on three challenging action datasets when compared to baseline approaches. An added feature allows the system to identify relevant video segments for rare action instances, demonstrating high F1 scores on three rare action recognition tasks.

The 2021 Image Similarity Challenge held in conjunction with CVPR yielded promising results, drawing participation from international teams. This challenge aimed to uncover novel aspects of image forgery through innovative approaches. Employing a straightforward objective, the challenge revealed state-of-the-art performance that has significant implications for practical applications. In addition to evaluations, the challenge also facilitated the creation of a comprehensive, high-quality dataset consisting of 1,600,000 forged images, the largest of its kind available thus far. This dataset, named the Mega Forgery Dataset, offers valuable features including detailed anatomical structures, allowing for in-depth analysis into the effects of image manipulation techniques. The challenge also garnered an impressive 96 algorithmic innovations in image manipulation detection, surpassing the previous year's total, highlighting their potential for future improvement. The challenge is made available on https://is-cvpr21.chalearn.org/.

This work explores degeneration parabolic equations with significant metabolic processes, examining external disturbance effects and systemic breakdown mechanisms near the boundary. It investigates the primary factors contributing to systemic failure and analyzes the impact of individual cell behavior on this phenomenon, using the stable metastable state of the system to illustrate persistence. The study culminates in a discussion on systemic failure due to spatial degradation, using the example of a membrane covered in various cell types to illustrate the dependence of boundary behavior on cell distribution patterns. It specifically considers a degenerate reaction-diffusion model with a porous membrane influenced by external disturbances, where the membrane degradation accelerates as diffusion properties decrease.

This research aimed to examine the energy distribution of a nuclear substance exposed to an intense magnetic field through the Light Cone Quantization concept. The study employed variational variations of the Hartree-Fock and Bogoliubov approaches to an average approximation in its methodology. The chosen nuclear substance was $^{208}$Pb with 6 quarks per nucleon accounting for its non-valence quarks. Results indicate that in the absence of a magnetic field, the energy distribution of the nuclear substance aligns with its experimental energy, while the introduction of a strong magnetic field led to shifts in the energy distribution. Notably, this effect was found to be more significant at the high momentum end. Furthermore, the study observed a correlation between the intensity of the magnetic field and the offset in the energy distribution.

A common issue in distributed machine learning is balancing communication efficiency and data privacy. To address this challenge, we have created an algorithm that achieves both efficient communication and private training. Our approach involves the model, REC, which allows training to occur locally without sharing data, while controlling the training results to enhance privacy and restrict potential leaks of the model. This algorithm acts as a shield, controlling the output of the model and the results it produces to maintain privacy. Our approach was successful, as it not only maintains the same level of performance as models trained without any restrictions, but also allows training to occur within a fraction of the time compared to models without any restrictions. Our approach was tested across various environments, finding that it can adapt to different environments, such as environments where the model or results can be accessed by third parties, among others. Our approach was successful, as it achieved a 90% reduction in the amount of data that needs to be shared during the training process. Our approach was further validated, as it achieved a 20% reduction in the amount of data that needs to be shared during the training process through the compression of data. Our approach has been made available as an open-source project, providing an environment that allows developers to test and validate the algorithm. Our approach has been successful, as it has received interest and attention from companies, as they are looking for ways to either improve or create private and secure environments for their data.

New far-ultraviolet images of a 160-square-degree area within the Taurus-Auriga complex have been released which cover the FUV wavelength range of 910-910+θ (where θ is roughly 70 degrees) relative to the Sun's direction. These images were observed as part of the GALEX mission and form part of an initiative to create a comprehensive far-ultraviolet sky survey. The data collected will serve multiple purposes including the location of extreme Lyman-α emitters, the tracking of bright O-type stars, and the acquisition of far-ultraviolet data for the purpose of atmospheric calibration. Additionally, the data will enable scientists to refine models predicting the Lyman-α dispersal of nearby stars, and the data will be accessible online for other missions to use.

Structured tables in documents like contracts, receipts, and receipts are invaluable for understanding and operating processes, yet naturally speaking language is often unreliable and overly verbose. Machines struggle to accurately identify table contents within scanned and printed documents, often failing due to illogical layouts, illogical hierarchies, and language ambiguities. Modern document processing techniques, primarily based on machine learning, can analyze human language, yet remain limited in tackling diverse table types, even after significant advancements in recent years. Our approach, centered on graph neural networks, effectively identifies and interpretes tables within complex PDF files, supplementing existing research in the field.

This research extends the theory of cognitive complexity, specifically relabeling it as 'cognitive layers,' to study multi-phase games where one player lacks complete information. We define a hierarchy of cognitive layers based on the level of information available to the uncertain player. Building on existing theory of zonotopes, we explore the properties of cognitive layers in partially informed games and derive two key principles: the Uniqueness Theorem and the Inclusion Postulate. These principles allow us to establish that the sum of cognitive layers achieved by iteratively applying the abode transformation is unique, and the abode transformation of a cognitive layer yields a subset that is inherently tighter than the original set. To validate our findings, we provide a intuitive example of a two-phase game involving two players. Additionally, this study also discusses partially informed games but does not explore their specific characteristics.

Estimating population density is crucial for various applications such as navigation, agriculture, environmental studies, disaster response, and reconnaissance. Populations often congregate around infrastructure like roads, buildings, and farmlands which leave recognizable patterns on satellite imagery. By utilizing transfer learning with an existing model, our approach achieves a population density estimation framework (PDE) that produces highly accurate results, demonstrating robust resilience. Our data augmentation techniques allow the framework to thrive in unforeseen scenarios, resulting in accurate population density models with limited optimization. The results highlight the effectiveness of our approach, particularly in urban environments, and its potential to adapt to real-world scenarios in challenging conditions.

To speed up the process of answering membership queries in large datasets, a novel, secure collection protocol called Filtered Collection of Predicates (FCP) was introduced, which relies on the cooperation of a fully trusted collector and a privately informed client. In FCP, the collector generates and distributes a secure filter to the client, allowing them to answer membership queries securely. A subsequent variant of FCP, known as Estimated Membership Query Filters (EMQF), was introduced, which enables the client to answer membership queries using an unofficial filter provided by the collector. In this paper, we explore a new concept, a false positive free (FPF) collection, which aims to eliminate the risk of incorrect positive query results for membership queries. We outline a strategy for creating a secure FPF collection and demonstrate its application through the development of a novel collection protocol, PFCP. By comparing the performance of PFCP to other existing protocols, including FCP and a variant of EMQF, our results demonstrate the practical value of eliminating incorrect positive query results, particularly when data sizes are constrained due to storage or bandwidth limitations. A key advantage of PFCP is its ability to either match or surpass the security and performance of its counterparts, depending on specific security parameters.

We investigate a process known as laser-induced three-body recombination in a specific gas of bosonic rubidium-85. Utilizing a quantum mechanical model that utilizes a multi-conjugate gradient method to optimize light-matter interaction, we compute the resulting recombination spectrum. Our research reveals distinct features in the spectrum resulting from the simultaneous presence of both atomic and molecular states in the system. Notably, we identify an unusual dark peak within the spectrum, which occurs at a specific phase, and can be attributed to the unique coexistence of single- and two-atom molecular states in the system. This phenomenon emerges due to an interconversion facilitated by a laser field between atomic and molecular states with a zero-spin. This process bears resemblance to a spinor wavefunction conversion, and can be manipulated by adjusting the laser intensity to optimize dark peak visibility.

For multiple reasons such as the severe damage caused by hurricanes in the engineering field, people explore the interaction between multiple physical components to better understand the complex behavior of fluids and solids. The widespread use of particle-based models, such as SPH method, in simulating multi-phase flow and solid-liquid interaction has led to significant breakthroughs. However, the typical SPH model has limitations in handling solid-like materials due to its over-relaxation, resulting in unrealistic solid behavior. In order to better model the interaction between solid and multiple fluids, people have proposed various models, each with its own limitations. In this study, a new multi-scale framework is introduced by integrating a mesoscopic model into a macroscopic SPH model to simulate fluid-solid interactions. The framework uses a pressure-stress reduction model to simulate the interaction between solid and multiple fluids, as well as a multi-scale material model for solid modeling. The framework's accuracy has been verified through comparison with the analytical solution and experimentally tested single phase and two phase models. The framework's performance has also been demonstrated through the simulation of complex problems such as seepage around isolated and adjacent foundations.

Machine learning has driven significant advancements in both industry and science, though its full potential remains largely unexplored due to a significant limitation - the need for constant supervision and adjustment. This necessity results in substantial competition between developing new algorithms and refining them, hindering the discovery of novel concepts. Researchers from the University of California and Google have devised a method to overcome this constraint. Their approach, quantum instruction learning, enables the discovery and refinement of algorithms without supervision, a capability already demonstrated in quantum systems by the creation of a quantum-assisted learning circuit. This circuit not only accelerates existing machine learning algorithms but also facilitates the discovery and refinement of new ones, previously inaccessible due to the complexity associated with classical implementations. The researchers successfully implemented a quantum-assisted learning circuit on a 28-qubit processor and observed an exponential decrease in training time, a reduction that could potentially lead to significant advancements in research.

A recently developed neural TTS model named FastPitch can change pitch within speech sounds, improving a previous system's speed and clarity. However, increasing the pitch often results in less clear and less natural sounding speech. A new study used pitch shift models to improve pitch control in FastPitch. The researchers applied pitch shift models that were trained on a large database of speech to modify the pitch of FastPitch-generated speech. Results showed that combining these models with FastPitch produced more natural sounding speech with higher pitch control. A comparison of these results with a previous system found that the combination performed better in terms of speech quality and pitch accuracy.

This research explores the solution space for end-to-end spatiotemporal reasoning using pre-trained language models, and proposes the Hopper model, which executes multi-hop reasoning based on entity relationships. Hopper employs a novel filtering technique to eliminate unneeded entities and reasoning steps, thereby efficiently processing long sequences and multiple reasoning steps. Additionally, the model incorporates a unique mechanism to manage entity knowledge levels, which accommodates diverse knowledge quantities across different entities. Extensive evaluations conducted on several datasets demonstrate Hopper's superior performance in story understanding and spatiotemporal reasoning, particularly its capacity for multi-hop reasoning. Notably, Hopper's performance surpasses state-of-the-art results in StoryCloze by 9.11 points and in Charades MultiHop by 22.6, reaching 68.15 and 72.60 respectively. The model's implementation is accessible via the Hopper Repository at https://github.com/PrakashVitel/Hopper.

This statistical analysis focuses on the process where a $W$ boson is generated along with two electrons or muons, and additional bottom quarks. The data from this process were taken from proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV, courtesy of the CMS experiment, resulting in 137 fb$^{-1}$ worth of data collected over several years. By comparing the observed outcomes against theoretical models, the mass of the $W$ boson was determined to be 40.9289 GeV with minimal deviation, yielding a result that is in line with the currently accepted standard model.

With the advancement of communication technologies, it is becoming easier for people to stay connected regardless of physical distance, thanks to various communication tools. This paper introduces a novel research approach that evaluates the Quality of Experience (QoE) for remote controlling a Telepresence robot via a high-quality communication network. To achieve this, a sophisticated robot controller was designed that simulates an immersive experience. A non-linear feedback loop was implemented to replicate a viewer's emotional response when controlling the robot, including feelings of frustration and excitement. Trained human testers provided subjective ratings and objective measurements to help calibrate the QoE model, ensuring accurate predictions. Our research contributes an interactive QoE model, known as the TelQoE model, which simulates human emotions, providing a more comprehensive understanding of QoE for Telepresence robot control. The proposed model can be further utilized to study QoE for various robotic applications.

Data analysis in various scientific fields relies heavily on linear models. However, when dealing with data that comes from multiple sources, sources that are similar in nature, or sources with inconsistent measurements, traditional models often fall short. This can lead to inaccurate results, particularly in cases where the sample size isn't sufficient. To address these challenges, a robust analytical framework called Bayesian Hierarchical Models is developed. This method combines the strengths of Bayesian Statistics, allowing for the balance of model accuracy and uncertainty. By leveraging Bayesian Statistics, this framework offers a principled approach to accounting for complex uncertainties. The primary goal of this text is to provide an accessible introduction to using Bayesian Hierarchical Models for linear model analysis. To achieve this goal, a step-by-step explanation of the fundamental concepts of Bayesian Statistics is given, followed by a detailed exploration of the various components of Bayesian Hierarchical Models. The software package rblm is utilized to demonstrate the application of this framework to real-world data.

This paper introduces a model for the popular Mafia game that incorporates perfect public confirmation and hidden votes of disloyalty. Players with the most votes become part of the Mafia, and each player's loyalty is publicly revealed at specific intervals. The model's key assumption is that players tend to act defensively, especially during day-time when they can identify potential threats and safely eliminate them without worrying about being killed. As a result, it's shown that the probability of winning for townspeople and Mafia follows a ratio of approximately 49:51. This outcome can also be extended to more complex variants with multiple Mafia members.

This study focuses on the development of planetary systems with multiple large planets, and examines how these planets form and evolve within a disk environment. We analyzed two possible planet configurations: identical twin Jupiter-like planets and non-identical giant planets. The twin planets model involved creating 10,000 models with varying starting conditions, while the non-identical planets model involved creating 1,000 models. We discovered that the presence of a second massive planet acts as an accelerator for gas accumulation in the first planet, and that for the second planet, gas accumulation is often delayed. As a result, the twin planets model exhibited a bimodal distribution in terms of final planet mass, while the non-identical planets model showed an increased spread in final mass compared to individual models. The interaction between planets in both models resulted in a spiral density enhancement that could potentially lead to the creation of planetary ring systems. If a wide orbit configuration exists, it may cause an outward pressure wave that can reduce the gas available for further planet development.

The ability to achieve energy transfer between different parts of a system is widespread in nature, and is particularly important in the transfer of heat between components of a material.  A study on a thin film made of carbon nanotubes found that heat is transferred between different parts of the nanotubes through vibrations of the atoms, and not through a direct electric current.  An analysis using the phonon-assisted tunneling technique showed that vibrations with certain energy levels allow for the transfer of energy between different parts of the nanotubes, and this transfer of energy depends on the distance between the different parts.  An efficient transfer of energy between different parts of the nanotubes results in a significant change in the electronic properties of the nanotubes at high temperatures, and this change can be controlled by varying the separation between the different parts of the nanotubes.  A preliminary study on a thin film made of carbon nanotubes found that the energy transfer between different parts of the nanotubes has the potential to be used for thermoelectric applications that can be controlled at a nanoscale.

This research develops a novel approach to high-dimensional fuzzy clustering based on entropy-driven variable feature weight optimization. The proposed method involves assigning distinct weights to each feature according of its contribution to data variability, as measured by the Renyi entropy of inter-cluster distances. A fuzzy cluster model is derived for center optimization, and a two-stage initialization procedure established. Evaluation of the method showed that it outperforms state-of-the-art algorithms, including the low-dimensional case.

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models effectively combine the benefits of localized representations and robust global reconstruction skills. However, training these models can be challenging due to the 'deadlock' issue, where standard algorithms easily get stuck in suboptimal solutions. This paper explores the causes of the deadlock and proposes innovative parameterizations and optimization techniques to overcome this challenge. The proposed solutions are evaluated on a range of tasks, including point sets, graph-structured and relational data. Notably, the proposed methods are applied without any modifications to standard baselines, but rather by simply rearranging their internal structures. The resulting algorithms are universally applicable and have the potential to adapt to any type of expert model. Our experiments demonstrate that these algorithms consistently outperform state-of-the-art baselines, achieving more accurate results with a significant reduction in computation time.

We're exploring a connection between negative circuit evaluations and the properties of abelian varieties, specifically through the lens of degree 2 differentials. Like intermediate Jacobians, we're focusing on intermediate forms on intermediate Jacobians to understand general elements, despite their results being somewhat restrictive. As a further contribution, we're introducing a specific game-theoretic framework, called the token-firing game, to illustrate key results and understand the nature of rational elements within intermediate Jacobians. Furthermore, for classes related to hyperbolic Riemann surfaces, we're establishing a connection to rational divisor classes on associated cover curves. Lastly, building on D. Mumford's findings on Lefschetz-type theorems for intermediate Jacobians, we're extending his work to apply to intermediate forms.

Various quantum gravity theories suggest the possibility of symmetry disruption, 
where the laws of physics are altered at the quantum level, affecting identical states 
in a different way. To investigate this concept, researchers analyzed the cosmic 
birefringance phenomenon caused by the disruption of $U(1)$ symmetry in the $E_8 \times 
E_8$ grand unified theory and other models. They discovered that, if such disruption 
occurred on an observable scale, it would result in an exponentially increasing 
distortion of the photon polarization modes, leading to a contradiction of current 
observational constraints. In fact, even the smallest possible scale of symmetry 
disruption, one order of magnitude larger than the Planck scale, still exceeds 
experimental limits, indicating that symmetry disruption on this scale is 
exceedingly unlikely.

The recently discovered, ultraviolet-luminous stars within the aging globular cluster NGC 4147 are being studied using new data from the UVIT. This observation includes ten bright stars found on the upper right part of the cluster's color-magnitude diagram. Specifically, our data cover the far-UV and near-UV bands, offering a resolution of approximately 0.2 inches. Our analysis includes a detailed examination of the variable stars' far-UV and near-UV bands over a period of 1.6 years. This reveals six possible new blue horizontal branch stars, and we also found that five stars are likely members of the cluster. Two observed white dwarfs do not exhibit any near-UV variability and have temperatures ranging from 6300K to 6800K. This matches the known temperature range for their fellow cluster members. We also found that the ten bright stars follow a luminosity function that can be described by a composite of two distinct distributions. This includes a primary Gaussian peak centered at 10.3 magnitudes in the near-UV band, and a secondary, less common distribution at 8.8 magnitudes. Additionally, we found that the ten bright stars follow a near-UV color magnitude temperature. This reveals two distinct groups, one belonging to the blue horizontal branch and the other belonging to the subdwarf category.

The theory of b-foliations, an extension of foliations theory, offers an alternative to group actions, offering a broader framework for studying related invariants. We explore the concept of b-principle in the context of b-foliations, inspired by the principle of characteristic classes. When b-complexes with isotopy invariant b-foliations are given, we aim to find b-foliations with smaller leaves that share the same b-invariants. This research is guided by a simplified version of the Mumford Conjecture, modified for b-complexes, which we combine with Gromov's norm to reformulate as a more manageable theory. This leads to a homological criterion for when the b-stable holonomy group is finite. We also establish a simplified version of the Bogomolov-McQuillan Conjecture.

Generalization capability in deep learning models is influenced by two key aspects, 
coherentness and fairness. We explore the connection between these properties and 
sparsity in our deep feature space, particularly as it concerns transfer learning 
issues. For instance, related classes tend to cluster together while distant 
classes remain isolated within a compact feature representation. Conversely, 
unrelated classes should remain distant from each other, as would be expected in 
a sparse feature space. We develop novel metrics: coherentness (Co) and 
fairness (Fa), to quantify these properties. Furthermore, we introduce 
Generalization Score (GenS) which integrates Co and Fa into a single performance 
indicator. We demonstrate the practical value of GenS by using it to optimize 
training efficiency and evaluate the potential of GenS to enhance model 
generalization capacity.

Acoustic networks comprised of insects and humans have been shown to effectively disseminate information across spatial distances through a process that defies the constraints of the speed of sound. This phenomenon occurs due to the reciprocal interactions taking place within these systems and facilitated by the presence of intermediate entities, such as birds, which can transport information across shorter distances. Computational model simulations reveal that the rate of information dissemination is directly influenced by the network's configuration and the diverse roles assumed by the agents residing within it. This outcome is most evident in systems operating at an optimal level of organization, where the interconnected components work harmoniously to enhance and expedite the process. Conversely, network fragmentation or over-saturation result in hindered information dissemination speeds. This study employs computational modeling to elucidate the mechanisms governing these processes and validates the findings using empirical data collected from an acoustic monitoring system. The research presents a core hypothesis, positing that the intricate structure of biological networks assumes a pivotal role in their collective intelligence and behavioral manifestations.

The unique characteristics of a closed metric (d), fulfilling the condition that its exterior derivative ds is smaller than epsilontimesquare, lead to the existence of a constant, epsilon greater than zero. This constant exists such that within a ball of radius epsilon surrounding the metric (d), no other distinct metric, with a smaller or weaker exterior derivative, can exist. This constant, epsilon, directly relates to the initial metric, (d). Specifically, it is proportional to the square root of the eigenvalues' gap in the Laplacian-d operator, with a proportionality constant that transcends functional analysis bounds. This phenomenon shares a striking resemblance with random matrices, where the study of extreme eigenvalues often yields distinct metrics. Just as random matrices under certain conditions develop gaps in their eigenvalues, similar phenomena in the metric (d), such as scaling up the radius of the ball, result in metrics with larger and smaller constants, epsilontwo, proportional to the gap in their eigenvalues. Ultimately, this distinctiveness implies that within a ball of radius epsilontwo surrounding the metric (d), no other distinct metric, with a smaller or weaker exterior derivative, can exist.

The standard perturbation models have been the most widely used methods for analyzing the time-domain performance of wireless communication systems. A four-core discrete-time model is developed to provide a precise analysis of unamplified links' time-domain standard perturbation models. This model offers a straightforward representation of the discrete-time power transfer, allowing for the exploration of perturbation models' time-domain behavior. The accuracy of the proposed model is validated for various scenarios, including random, specific, and worst-case perturbations. This model showcases the impact of sampling rate on the time-domain behavior of the perturbation models.

The evasive nature of Android malware has long posed a significant threat to user privacy and device security by avoiding detection from security apps through various countermeasures. This study provides an in-depth analysis of how Android malware subverts the operating system's core components and the literature on anti-malware techniques to prevent detection. The analysis reveals the common evasive tactics employed by malware, which can then inform the development of effective security measures to counter such attacks. In addition, this study proposes a potential anti-malware approach based on the concept of "evasion spaces". This proposed method is distinguished by its comprehensive nature, covering all Android app systems, and by bypassing certain security mechanisms that can compromise detection accuracy. This study, which aims to provide a thorough understanding of evasion attacks on the Android operating system, offers an extensive review of evasion attacks on Android apps, including the malware evasion space, malware evasion attacks, anti-malware techniques, and a potential anti-evasion space based on the concept of "evasion spaces". This study further explores future directions for research inspired by the concept of evasion spaces.

A reliable and flexible tool for managing computational clusters, called a "virtual cluster manager," is essential in science and engineering to leverage the power of distributed computing for solving complex problems.

Our experience in developing a virtual cluster manager for flow simulation on Google's cloud platform has led to significant challenges that will be discussed in terms of their solutions.

The resulting tool, called "Ozy," provides a set of APIs that allow developers to create new execution and scheduling strategies within the system, thereby enriching its capabilities.

By introducing Ozy, we have found that a virtual cluster manager is a missing component in the field of flow simulation software.

Our research demonstrates that Ozy's current implementation achieves a 50% reduction in latency and 30% reduction in overhead compared to alternative methods on Google's cloud platform.

Furthermore, Ozy's modular design makes it compatible with a wide range of computational platforms, including those provided by Amazon Web Services, as of the date of its development.

The ground state of electrons in a certain five-fold degenerate Landau level can be described by a Wigner-Mixing-Angle phase, occurring at a specific density and magnetic field, apart from trivial cases where symmetry is broken. By combining density-matrix renormalization group simulations and continuous-time quantum Monte Carlo methods, we found this reentrant phase transition occurs at a moderate level of electron-electron interaction. This phase features a quantized Hall conductivity, but differs from the conventional fractional quantum Hall states as it does not exhibit a well-defined local entropy and confined excitation.

Our analysis reevaluates the event rates of primordial black holes detected by the LIGO-Virgo collaboration, considering a wider range of characteristics than in the initial study. The review begins by identifying the Thakurta metric parameter space characterized by specific evolutionary stages of cosmological black holes, including isolated, interacting, and merged entities. The findings indicate that cosmological black holes in the mass range of the LIGO events cannot survive for extended periods due to interactions that transfer energy, suggesting the Thakurta parameter space is inaccessible. The implications are that the event rates of primordial black holes remain unchanged from previous estimates, with approximately $0.01$ events per day from a 20--40 solar mass binary system in the horizon volume. The review concludes with suggestions for verifying cosmological black hole characteristics through electromagnetic observations of binary systems.

The formation of planets from pebbles is a theory that's gaining traction. However, the accumulation process is thought to occur primarily in areas with low pebble velocities. Moreover, velocities are influenced by the density structure of the protoplanetary disk. A computational investigation examined how density fluctuations impact pebble velocities and, in turn, the formation of planets. In regions with significant density, pebble velocities can become high enough to hinder planet growth, whereas velocities can be favorable in areas with low density. As a result, the density structure of the disk has the potential to significantly impact planetary formation.

We investigate how the computational complexities of training procedures and data accessibility affect the success of non-linear regression models. Unlike linear regression, where the number of data points needed to achieve low bias approaches infinity with increasing dimensions, we find that finite data sets can be successful in high-dimensional spaces for certain training methods, albeit with high variance. This success is tied to the training algorithm's computational complexity. Notably, this contrasts with the traditional perspective that emphasizes the importance of data quantity over its inadequacy due to dimensionality issues. Our research specifically evaluates the statistical effectiveness of two trainings methods: an inefficient, constant-time "random feature" method and a more efficient, iterative least-squares "gradient descent" method. We discover that the successful high-dimensional regression models are easily generalized and have low bias and variance. This phenomenon is attributed to the differences in computational complexity rather than the well-known statistical guarantees related to data diversity. Furthermore, this example highlights the significance of considering the training process's computational aspects in high-dimensional regression models.

We demonstrate the existence of Bohr structures of countably infinite abelian groups with the operation of summing natural numbers, specifically those in the form of $\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} G_i \times F_i$, where each $G_i$ is a finite group and each $F_i$ is an infinite torsion-free group. We also prove the converse, stating that any Bohr structure of this type originates from a set of groups that satisfy this description. Additionally, we define and examine three classes of sets, each representing the domain of possible Bohr structures of countable groups resulting from repeated sums of finite, zero-dimensional groups; infinite torsion groups; and torsion-free groups, respectively. We prove these classes form a hierarchy and provide examples of sets within each level. We also show that taking the product of sets from the second level effectively generates sets from the first level.

The dial-a-ride problem with limited capacity vehicles serves as a component of more complex urban transportation systems including ride-hailing and ride-sharing platforms. These platforms' popularity has continued to rise, prompted by changes in consumer behavior and significantly reduced costs. This research explores a specific variant of the dial-a-ride problem where drivers' idle time is accounted for and we have determined it to be an NP-hard problem. A new Branch and Trim algorithm is proposed for solving smaller-scale instances of the problem more efficiently. Compared to previous solutions, its performance has surpassed previous results by 25% and has the added benefit of allowing researchers to trim unnecessary solutions from the branch and trim tree, thus reducing overall computation time.

The emergence of e-commerce listings where multiple information sources coexist has brought about a growth in tasks such as product classification, clustering and visual-related word description. Current solutions rely heavily on basic visual features or learn complex visual features using vast amounts of labeled data, but this poses significant challenges for practical applications. To overcome these obstacles, we propose an innovative information-integrated pre-training method, designed to leverage product knowledge for enhanced e-commerce vision tasks. Our new framework combines multiple signal types, including image, text and feature, and utilizes an advanced multi-modal design that recognizes and adapts to different types of information. To promote the sharing of cross-modal information, we incorporate a memory module that temporarily stores information from one modality and makes it accessible to others. To further optimize our model's adaptability, we allow the information stored in the memory to decay over time. Our proposed method excelled in numerous e-commerce vision tasks and surpassed the competition in several key metrics. The source code for our model has been made available at https://github.com/kuangyang1988/KNOM.

Every year, a substantial number of elderly individuals experience cognitive decline.
It's estimated that approximately 9.6 million people worldwide live with dementia, with
this number set to rise significantly as the global population ages if current trends
continue unchanged. Early diagnosis and understanding of the progression to Alzheimer's
are crucial for effective treatment and management. However, conventional methods
involve expensive scans and blood tests, limiting widespread use due to cost and
availability constraints. Our research aims to develop an innovative approach by
combining data from MRI and blood tests to create a universal tool for predicting
cognitive decline using deep learning techniques. By leveraging Deep InfoMax, we
created a universal brain model reflecting general brain structure, disregarding
individual identities, conditions, and specific data sources. This model can then
be combined with condition-specific models, trained separately, which we've dubbed
the identity-aware model. Our findings demonstrate that the Deep InfoMax model
exceeds the performance of a multiple linear regression model based on MRI and blood
tests, reaching 0.8541 AUC for predicting Alzheimer's disease based solely on brain MRI
scans. This breakthrough has significant potential to lay the groundwork for a
universal diagnostic test utilizing MRI scans to forecast dementia progression with
the potential for widespread application.

In natural language processing, a long-standing challenge is accurately capturing the underlying semantic meaning of text, a task closely linked to human reasoning abilities. To tackle this problem, previous studies have employed numerous techniques and networks, from simple feed-forward layers to complex recurrent and transformer networks. Despite some success with the latter in capturing semantic relationships, they have significant drawbacks, such as requiring vast amounts of data and being ineffective at handling tasks that involve sequential processing. This paper proposes the interaction-driven recurrent network (IRN) for semantic interpretation, an architecture that integrates the interaction of multiple neural networks with a recurrent neural network. This integration enables better capture of the context through deeper and multi-level interactions between words, allowing for more accurate and efficient semantic representation. The IRN architecture outperforms previous models in numerous benchmark tests for semantic interpretation tasks.

We have developed more precise theoretical models for the spin-orbit interaction in materials with strong electron interactions, applying these to key 5$d$-transition metal oxides. For the model with critical $U$ terms in the metal's local site, the spin-orbit interaction is directly proportional to the overall electron exchange energy, incorporating both the metal's $U$ coupling and the lateral $U_{int}$ interaction between adjacent sites. For the more complex Kondo lattice case, the proportionality holds for large $U$ coupling values, but in the opposite direction, requiring a reconsideration of previous research findings on the spin-orbit interaction in these types of materials. We've also developed a more straightforward method for calculating the spin-orbit interaction in these systems of strongly correlated electrons and explored their implications for the relevant heavy fermion compounds and topological insulator materials.

In this context, the shadow substance formalism is applied within a conformal space-time framework. Shadow substance proposals have two distinct variants, a classical variant and a quantum variant. The classical variant is based on a straightforward mapping, whereas the quantum variant leverages the concept of a density matrix to describe the metastable states of a system. The focus is on exploring quantum variant applications, which involve embedding an equilibrium state called the shadow sector within a broader, out-of-equilibrium state known as the source sector. This is accomplished using a time-variant metric, where the source sector is described by its proper time, thereby giving rise to a new, effective metric for the shadow sector at stationary states. The effective metric's eigenvalues can be used to map the shadow sector's spacetime geometry, as illustrated by a few simple examples.

Several renowned medical imaging AI models have raised red flags over potential safety issues after being deployed without proper evaluation of their performance in real-world settings. The existing methods for validating medical image analysis algorithms often rely on overly simplistic assumptions, such as the data used for testing being identical in nature to the data used for training. In reality, this distribution shift often doesn't occur, and as a result, there's an urgent need for reliable assessment tools that can accommodate the complexities involved in medical data sets and the presence of untestable hypotheses. We propose an innovative framework based on conformal forecasting that can accurately assess the performance of image analysis algorithms under various types of distribution shifts, including complex scenarios involving multiple test distributions. The proposed approach is capable of providing accurate estimates by leveraging the output predictions from multiple models trained on different data sets. The reliability of this approach was demonstrated through empirical simulations involving chest X-ray images and the accurate assessment of a test model's performance based on predictions from training and testing data. The impact of using an inaccurate "nearness" measure in the model assessment was also studied using the Hausdorff distance as an alternative, which in turn led to the investigation of its potential in aiding diagnostic tasks as a form of semi-supervised learning tool.

A new, ultra-low interaction "repulsive" force is being applied between a specific set of atoms, where any standard interaction is replaced with a uniquely repulsive force field. This replacement is between specific sets of atoms as defined by the "Stiff Base" potential type within the force field. This unique set of interactions was tested within an existing DNA model system built using the CHARMM36m potential type. This potential type was used to simulate a 10 nanosecond DNA simulation using the Molecular Dynamics method. This unique set of interactions was discovered to significantly improve the accuracy of simulations by significantly increasing the range of possible DNA conformations that are able to be modeled. This unique set of interactions was discovered to significantly improve the overall accuracy of simulations by increasing the range of possible DNA conformations that are able to be modeled without significantly increasing the overall cost of simulations in terms of computational resources required.

In the past decade, considerable attention has been given to the role of the Active Numerical System in understanding mathematics. Research suggests that numerical actions are often easier when patients face low levels of abstract risk, as quantified by the ANS entropy. However, theoretical foundations supporting the importance of ANS entropy are still in their early stages. This paper aims to establish a more comprehensive understanding by defining it as a measure of how well the mind compresses information and as such, enhances learning and pattern detection. We argue that ANS entropy is specifically important for recognizing numerical patterns, and propose the importance of a critical threshold of ANS entropy for numerical and mathematical processing.

To model the dielectric behavior of cement-based materials and their pore fluids accurately, it's essential to consider the composition and temperature of the pore fluid. A simplified approach representing the pore fluid as a mixture of water, electrolyte, and cement-based substances in solution is utilized, yielding a dielectric coefficient that follows a Creep model. This behavioral pattern is the result of the movement of ions in the complex fluid. This model enables the dielectric behavior of cement-based materials and their pore fluids to be closely mimicked through experimental data comparison. Furthermore, the relative dielectric coefficient of the pore fluid correlates with the total bound water, as determined experimentally.

To incorporate heavy-heavy clusters into lattice QCD calculations, a novel study approach has been established, leveraging effective field theory and dimensional regularization to address the associated mathematical challenges thoroughly, thereby allowing for accurate lattice QCD calculations across a wide range of energy levels. The research presents detailed calculations for two heavy-heavy clusters, comprising bottom-quark and top-quark combinations, which are crucial for understanding various astrophysical and particle physics phenomena. The findings provide a comprehensive framework for applying dimensional regularization in this context and also discuss its application to lattice QCD via the moving frame technique.

The utilization of drones in military operations has increased significantly, driven by advancements in technology, resulting in improved performance, reduced costs, and widespread accessibility. These improvements, however, have primarily been achieved through empirical trial and error rather than being based on scientific principles. The present study sets out to assess the progress in military drone development through the analysis of related texts, employing methods from natural language processing and semantic search. By examining news articles and press releases from 2015 to 2020, the study employs two methodologies: a quantitative approach focusing on keyword distribution and a qualitative, in-depth analysis of semi-structured topics. The findings indicate that military drone advancements have largely been driven by cost-reducing factors, with life-cycle expenses expected to decrease substantially, but at a slower rate than technological and feasibility hurdles to implementation. The study's results provide valuable insights for decision-makers and researchers, highlighting areas for future focus where significant benefits are likely to derive from further investigation.

The relationship between large-scale structure observations and cosmological parameters can be studied in depth using the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest and cross-validation with galaxy surveys. This research introduces a novel statistical method that calculates a parameter by combining the Lyman-$\alpha$ correlation functions and is highly sensitive to fluctuations. This parameter exhibits a strong relationship with thermal broadening but minimal dependence on other factors. Using simulations, we analyzed the Lyman-$\alpha$ correlation functions from two different quasars and compared them with a proxy derived from galaxy clustering, finding consistency at a 2σ confidence level. This is the first time that the Lyman-$\alpha$ correlation functions have been directly compared to galaxy clustering data, and it sets a new standard for combining observations from two distinct methods.

Researchers at Fermilab have successfully conducted an experiment where charged beams transfer emittances across different planes. The experiment involved a transverse emittance exchange that preserved beam intensity, involved beta functions of up to 2.5 meters, and resulted in minimal loss, below one percent, of the beam's energy. The study also demonstrated the feasibility of an innovative technique to observe emittance scattering through processes involving strong magnetic fields and also revealed that small errors in setup didn't impede the emittance exchange efficiency by much. Following this breakthrough, the researchers were able to test a new mechanism for emittance exchange, one that utilizes a hybrid approach combining both a strong and weak defocusing component. The success of this two-step process, known as a non-Abelian emittance exchange, not only confirms a long-predicted phenomenon but also opens a new path for future beam research and experiments.

Current research on autonomous vehicles' future trajectory prediction tends to focus on forecasting the entire path, but this doesn't account for the fact that the predicted route can change depending on various interactions, such as lane changes or yellow lights. Moreover, just forecasting the entire path may not be enough to capture the complexity of social interactions that vehicles encounter. To address these limitations, our study involves creating two new modules: the first one enables the prediction of the path segment relevant to the current time and context, while the second considers social interactions that might lead to a change in the predicted path segment. These modules are based on the concepts of sequential neural networks and a socially-aware rethinking framework, and we've also adapted the CVAE framework to allow the model to forget past information as it moves forward in time. Our analysis shows that the proposed modules outperform existing models in terms of accuracy and also provides a new way of visually understanding trajectory forecasts.

Over the past forty years, researchers have utilized various information-theoretic measures to evaluate the complexity of systems, such as interconnected networks and dynamical systems. Our study, however, takes a unique approach by directly comparing these measures within the context of a specific system, namely a two-layer Boltzmann machine. Our choice of system allows us to gradually adjust its parameters and observe the resulting changes in complexity. Specifically, we employed three information-theoretic measures: total Shannon information entropy, conditional Shannon entropy, and mutual information. Our results reveal that these measures often align in simple cases but exhibit discrepancies in more complex scenarios. Moreover, we demonstrate that these measures can both support and contradict one another.

This research proposes a novel technique for hand gesture recognition that enables real-time, remote communication between humans and a swarm of drones. A compact, deep learning-based model is employed to analyze hand movements as they change over time, allowing complex commands to be issued with minimal verbal or visual feedback. Experimental evaluations of our model, applied to Keck Wave Handwriting Dataset and a custom "hand gesture" dataset, demonstrate a competitive recognition rate of 73.94% using frame sequences. Furthermore, we provide a detailed description of a drone swarm platform that integrates this recognition model, allowing for effortless command issuing with minimal visual interference.

The human blood contains numerous cells that are crucial for the body's defense and regulatory systems, including red blood cells, which transport oxygen, white blood cells, which fight infections, and platelets, which enable blood coagulation. These different cells can be identified using an analysis called differential interference contrast, or DIc image. However, even experienced microscopists struggle to accurately classify these cells in DIc images. This problem has been addressed by developing and testing a novel machine learning-based method for automatically classifying blood cells in DIc images. This method relies on a specific type of neural network called a convolutional neural network, or CNN. We created and trained four separate CNNs on different subsets of a comprehensive blood cell image dataset and combined them to create a single, merged network. This approach significantly enhanced our method's accuracy, with our merged network achieving remarkable classification rates of roughly 98% for monocytes, lymphocytes, basophils, neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils, and platelets from DIc images. We compared our method to other state-of-the-art techniques, or benchmarks, including a sophisticated blood cell classification method developed by a company called Haodong Chen et al., and a novel, advanced image processing method developed by a researcher named Alaa A. E. et al. We also tested our method using a different image analysis technique, or algorithm, to provide a comprehensive comparison with established classification methods. This comparison validated our method's

Our approach presents a unified method for assembling the ground state of the Hubbard model, a quantum system, from its non-ground state initial state. The method is based on an extension of the counterdiabatic protocol (CDP), which normally requires the system's Hamiltonian be decomposed into two separate terms. The proposed method generates a new Hamiltonian parameterization, whose driving speed is carefully calibrated to guide the system from its initial state to the ground state of its own Hamiltonian. The method does not rely on knowing the ground state wavefunction, but instead uses a variational principle to determine the optimal Hamiltonian parameterization, making it a self-consistent technique. The method also has the property that it excites fewer non-ground states, effectively steering the system towards its target state with minimal 'disturbance'. The method was tested to converge to the ground state of the Hubbard model from a non-ground state for a finite number of driving steps, as well as being robust against certain types of driving speed errors. The study also found that the method's performance improves as the number of parameterizing terms increases. The method, with its potential for assembling the ground state of any Hubbard model configuration, can be extended to the study of one-dimensional spin-1/2 fermions.

A new, fast method for image decoration, high-velocity decoration, is developed based on the change in color temperature. This approach models how different regions of an image, according to their color temperature, interact and change as the image moves. Various images have distinct color temperature ranges due to their diverse content; for instance, landscapes with blue skies have a distinct range distinct from that of violent high-temperature situations. High-velocity decoration is unique in that it is affected by an image's internal structure of different color temperatures, leading to intricate and complex movement effects when simulated. Unlike other simulation methods, this approach can also create unique visual effects in specific scenarios, such as a blue sky turning red due to an explosion. This phenomenon is unique in that it is driven by the interaction between different image structures of varying color temperatures, rather than simply being a result of external factors like explosions.

The process of expanding a function in a series, known as the Taylor expansion, can be simplified for complex functions, and this simplified process can be used to identify a pattern allowing for much faster computation of higher-order terms.

Given a surface shaped like a certain geometric pattern and attached to it is a network of curved lines called Harbinge graphs, this research develops new methods to understand how to fill in the gaps of the surface while preserving its original characteristics. As a result, we obtain novel proofs of several important results in the field of topology and geometric measure theory. Our techniques apply to surfaces of a specific type with bounded curvature and can also be used in more general scenarios by using a specific concept of branching.

A novel concept for a table-top laboratory-scale all-photon quantum source is presented, leveraging the synergy between monochromatic laser photons and keV-scale X-ray photons in a high-intensity plasma environment. The combination of electrostatic and Stark Stark shifts, along with other external fields, allows for the precise tuning of atomic energy levels to achieve significant electric-dipole transitions in the keV energy range. The generation of tunable, narrow-linewidth photons in the keV range is demonstrated through experimental observations of enhanced photoionization cross-sections and nonresonant M\"{o}ssbauer effect spectra. The resulting photons in the keV range exhibit characteristics necessary for quantum information applications, including the capability to be coherently manipulated, modulated, and entangle with other photons. Furthermore, the source can produce entangled triplets of photons spanning an energy range from a single photon to a pair of photons, opening possibilities for quantum information applications, spectroscopy, and precision measurement. The source can also be adapted for the production of rare optical photons in the 1 nanometer range, enabling optical quantum information at the single atom level.

Several constraints have been imposed on the Two Higgs Doublets Model in light of the fact that the approach to the chromo-electric instability region is being explored more closely.  It's known that as the pseudoscalar boson mass decreases, the model's predictions for the vacuum stability become predictions themselves.  In this paper, the model's predictions for the pseudoscalar boson mass are driven by specific cutoffs related to the instability region.  It's also been found that constraints on the ratio of light and heavy boson masses along with their difference dictate the model's predictions for this pseudoscalar boson mass.  In addition to these findings the model's predictions for certain low energy reactions and its double beta decay signature are influenced by the same parameter, the light and heavy boson mass ratio.  It's been found that for certain values of this ratio, the model's predictions remain relatively unchanged, however this is not the case when the ratio varies significantly.  In fact certain experimental bounds are found to limit the model's predictions for this ratio and consequently the model's predictions for the model's parameters and its various physical properties.

RDF data describes information using subject-predicate-object statements, whereas data management systems often represent information in a structured format, such as XML or JSON. A recent proposal known as Shape Expressions seeks to define constraints and data organization in XML documents similar to schema definitions in databases. This research outlines transformations to convert data from a structured XML or JSON format to RDF, enabling the application of various existing approaches to validate, modify, and migrate XML or JSON documents while also providing examples of validating shaped RDF data.

A new field called shape analysis in statistics is focused on studying the form of data distributions without making assumptions about their type or dimensionality. Previous research has introduced the StoNED algorithm for non-convex shape analysis, enabling the identification of a shape boundary based on a representative dataset. Building on this, a new Python library pyStoNED provides a structured implementation of the StoNED algorithm, enhancing its computational efficiency and user experience through optimized programming. This package offers a range of tools and examples to facilitate shape analysis, accompanied by a user guide that outlines the steps for conducting a shape study using pyStoNED.

In the standard model, the Higgs boson is a crucial component that gives mass to fundamental particles, but it can be extended through various theories, such as gauge Higgs theories, to create the subtle Higgs concept. As the LHC continues to produce a vast amount of data, it is essential to search for the subtle Higgs within the $t \bar t \phi$ production process. This study provides a comprehensive review of these searches and offers alternative approaches to improve these simulations and searches. To compare results, we have created a benchmark model incorporating the subtle Higgs modification of the standard model Higgs boson. Furthermore, we have developed two simulated search strategies using the $\text{HLLE}$ method to highlight the effectiveness of these approaches in detecting the subtle Higgs. Using the standard model $t \bar t \phi$ process, we have demonstrated that these search strategies can be utilized to set a limit of 0.0355 for the Higgs field's coupling to fermions, based on the 139 fb$^{-1}$ luminosity of the LHC. We have also shown the sensitivity of these strategies in detecting the subtle Higgs up to a mass of 400 GeV for different scenarios.

Pretrained language models (PLMs) have transformed the realm of NLP by delivering exceptional results across various tasks. Traditionally, PLMs have been fine-tuned with abundant supervised data, but research is shifting towards exploring their potential in unsupervised and few-shot learning scenarios. These emerging areas of study aim to push the boundaries of what PLMs can accomplish with either no supervision or minimal data, complemented by minimal, often synthetic, in-context prompts. This study delves into the current state of unsupervised and few-shot analysis powered by PLMs, covering the state-of-the-art methods, key challenges, and proposed novel methods and future research directions. Furthermore, we provide a tutorial on reproducing the main experiments from the referenced papers, employing the Transformers library to leverage the capabilities of BERT, Roberta, and other related models.

The accuracy of spoken word recognition technology has significantly improved in recent years, enabling its widespread application across platforms, including mobile devices, voice assistants, and digital archiving projects. In fields like historical research and linguistic science, access to spoken language data is often restricted to specific regions, languages, or time periods, necessitating the development of customized speech recognition systems. These systems, however, are frequently built using proprietary tools, which complicate data exchange, replication, and citation. To address these issues, we've created Aspen, an open-source German speech recognition system based on the MuMa model.

The characteristics of Be-type stars in the 30 Doradus region were investigated through spectroscopic analysis by the FEROS instrument. An improved version of the B-type star spectral classification has been created that takes into account the characteristics of strong helium lines, and a study found 41 Be-type stars within the area with spectral types ranging from B1 to B5, and a projected rotational velocity of less than 200 km/s. The mass range of the Be-type stars is estimated to be 12-18 solar masses, and a specific subgroup (<15 solar masses) was identified that might have a shorter lifetime. The evidence suggests a binary or unconventional origin for two of the Be-type stars. The study also found a density of Be-type stars varying across different areas of the region, and a specific pattern could be seen in the distribution of spectral types across different areas, consistent with the shape of the region.

Inverse text standardization aims to identify the original formatting used in a piece of text, specifically its case, language, and encoding. This formatting can be crucial for text analysis, but existing methods tend to be limited in their effectiveness due to the complexity involved. To overcome this, we suggest employing data augmentation techniques to improve the performance of inverse text standardization models. By generating and incorporating more examples, we can enhance the models' ability to effectively convert underformatted text. Compared to other approaches, our method demonstrates better results, as evidenced by experiments involving different data augmentation techniques and several inverse standardization methods.

This document presents a sharp inequality involving the first eigenvalue of the Hermite operator when subject to a Robin condition on the boundary. Specifically, we find that the optimal configuration is a half-shelf structure. Furthermore, we examine the limit case where the parameter governing the Robin condition becomes zero or negative infinity.

Traditional kernel-based methods employ fixed, non-adaptive distributions to model data.  In contrast, numerous recent approaches leverage learned, dynamic probability models to capture complex data relationships.  We present a new class of kernel variants that fall somewhere in between these two strategies, leveraging a standard, fixed form for most of the data but adapting it for key subsets.  This research is grounded in a NLP context where NMT-based prior knowledge can inform kernel construction.  We show that an unsupervised kernel derived from a fixed, mutli-modal distribution, and a new, related family of distributions that ensure exchangeability under data-class conditional constraints, provide significant performance gains in supervised and semi-supervised learning applications.

Recent discoveries in non-Hermitian topological systems have seen significant advancements or predictions. Research suggests that the topological characteristics of one-dimensional systems hosting two-gap models can be reduced to either a zero-gap or a one-gap model, depending on correlation effects. This outcome is due to the interactions between correlated electrons, which modify the topological indicators - namely, the electron's fractional boundary density of states and its bulk fractional anomalous Hall effect - potentially eliminating the system's topological features. This reduction occurs as the correlated electrons convert the continuous topological features into either a zero-gap or a one-gap topology.

This research introduces a method to incorporate social speaker characteristics and personality into English synthetic speech. We have developed a personality-quasi system, similar to QuasiQ, which assesses personality traits based on spoken responses. The system's trait assessments for a particular speaker are refined through calibration, which corrects any discrepancies between the trait ratings and actual speaking style. The improved trait set serves as a more accurate guideline for generating synthetic speech that reflects the speaker's unique personality and communication habits. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated by pairs of speakers exhibiting distinct personality and communication patterns. The results show that incorporating the corrected trait characteristics through speech style calibration significantly enhances the perceptual authenticity of synthetic speech.

A variant of the Standard Model featuring a spontaneously broken $Z'_B-L$ symmetry, along with left-handed components of all fermions, is examined in a context where the residual $A_4$ symmetry remains unbroken. Within this framework, a minimal model has been developed that accounts for the generation of masses to both charged fermions and neutrinos via the same, non-charged under $U(1)_{B-L}$ singlet field, while also explaining the existence of luminous dark matter. Although the model incorporates additional constraints beyond those of the Standard Model, its parameter space remains largely within the bounds set by the current data, particularly for a specific range of values in the soft supersymmetry scale.

In a triaxial nucleus, low-lying quadrupole vibrations can be characterized by intrinsic motions characterized as a one-dimensional Brownian motion in a simple model. Building on this, a more comprehensive model is developed to describe the intrinsic motion of triaxial nuclei, incorporating the effects of a minimum length in quantum mechanics. The intrinsic motion of triaxial nuclei is driven by a one and two dimensional overdamped Brownian motion, enabled by a minimum length in quantum mechanics. Our study provides a detailed classification of the lowest triaxial quadrupole vibrations in $^{124}$Xe and $^{126}$Xe nuclei, based on intrinsic motion, and determines the minimum length in quantum mechanics, specifically between 0.7-0.8 fm. The sequence of quadrupole vibrations in $^{124}$Xe and $^{126}$Xe nuclei can be accurately predicted using the intrinsic motion of triaxial nuclei, and the effects of a minimum length in quantum mechanics. Our work offers a new classification of the lowest triaxiity quadrupole vibrations, characterized as a diffusive or rotational or mixed in nature. The first observed eigenvectors and eigenfrequencies of quadrupole vibrations in $^{124}$Xe and $^{126}$Xe nuclei can be accurately predicted, and the effects of a minimum length in quantum mechanics.
